Text | S.Li

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Hello everyone! It’s 2022, and I’m stealing some time to continue the ANC series. One thing has changed since the last article: I’ve moved back to China for work~ I now do R&D on spatial audio, but I keep a close eye on what’s happening with ANC headphones on the market, so if you’d like to swap notes, you are more than welcome! I also hope to write some explainers on spatial audio when I get the chance.

This article is mainly about a paper I presented at Internoise last year (Li, Schlieper and Peissig (2021): Semi-adaptive active noise cancellation headphones, Internoise 2021).

Earlier installments covered the differences between fixed (non-adaptive) and adaptive noise-cancelling headphones and how to design them. Fixed ANC headphones have one obvious hallmark, summed up in a word: stability! They have a certain take-it-easy attitude: “This is all the noise cancellation I’ve got, but I promise nothing will go badly wrong, like howling.” Adaptive ANC headphones are more of a headache. After adapting for a while they can achieve excellent noise reduction, but when conditions change, for example when the headphones are taken off or put back on, a large error can suddenly appear or the system can start to howl, and it needs time to converge again before it can cancel noise. If the parameters are tuned or set badly, the adaptive filter may never converge at all.

So I came up with the idea of combining adaptive and fixed filters, to improve the performance of ANC headphones while still guaranteeing the stability of the ANC system. This article deals with feedback ANC systems, but the method applies to feedforward (FF), feedback (FB) and hybrid ANC systems alike.

Figure 1 shows the hardware structure of feedback ANC headphones. xa(t) is the ambient noise and da(t) is the noise measured at the entrance to the ear canal. da(t) is effectively xa(t) after attenuation by the headphone shell. ya(t) is the anti-noise signal played back. These are all analog signals. e(n) and y(n) are, respectively, the measured residual noise and the generated anti-noise signal; these are digital signals. The latency introduced by AD/DA conversion is included in the simulations later on.

Figure 1: Hardware structure of feedback ANC headphones

Figures 2 and 3 show block diagrams of fixed and adaptive feedback ANC headphones. G(z) is the secondary path and W(z) is the feedback ANC filter. I covered these two classic block diagrams in an earlier article, along with how to design the filters, so I won’t repeat that here. For a refresher, see Everything you wanted to know about noise-cancelling headphones, part 3.

Figure 2: Block diagram of a fixed (non-adaptive) feedback ANC system

Figure 3: Block diagram of an LMS-based adaptive feedback ANC system

The pros and cons of the two approaches have been covered above and in earlier articles. To get the best of both, I designed a way of combining adaptive and fixed filters and named it the semi-adaptive feedback ANC system. Its rough structure is shown in Figure 4. The part inside the blue box is the adaptive ANC system; the part outside it is the fixed ANC system. The output signal of the overall ANC system is:

y(n)=ayfixed(n)+(1−a)yadap(n)

The outputs of the fixed and adaptive filters are weighted by a and 1 − a respectively. When a = 0, only the adaptive filter is active; conversely, when a = 1, only the fixed filter is active. The weight a is computed and updated automatically according to the state of the ANC system.

At the start, a = 1. The noise reduction may not be outstanding, but the ANC system is guaranteed to be stable. The adaptive filter’s output, yadap(n), makes no contribution because of the weighting (1 − a = 0), but it keeps adapting all the while. From the block diagram, the residual error of the adaptive part, e′(n), can be written as:

e′(n)=e(n)+ĝ*(y(n)−yadap(n))

where ĝ is the estimated secondary path (the one used when computing the filter), in the time domain.

We can then judge the state of the ANC system from the adaptive filter’s residual noise, e′(n), and the measured residual noise of the ANC system, e(n). If, over a period of time, RMS(e′(n)) > RMS(e(n)), the residual noise the adaptive filter would produce is larger than that of the overall ANC system as it stands. This can be read as a major change in the system’s state: the headphones suddenly being taken off or put on, being dropped, an abrupt change in the ambient noise and so on. So as soon as this happens, the output weight a is set to 1, cutting off the adaptive filter’s output to keep the ANC system stable. When RMS(e′(n)) < RMS(e(n)), the residual noise from the adaptive filter is likely to be smaller than the current residual noise of the ANC system, so the adaptive filter’s output can be given more weight (1 − a > 0). RMS stands for root mean square, by the way.

Figure 4: Block diagram of the semi-adaptive feedback ANC system

Now let’s look at the simulation results. We measured the secondary paths of a pair of over-ear headphones (the brand stays secret!) in different states. The measurements covered not only normal wear by different people but also special cases, such as the headphones lying on a table or not fully covering the ears. The median of these measurements served as the estimate Ĝ(z) used to compute the feedback filter. In the simulation, the secondary path was switched every 2 seconds (picking from the measured data set) to simulate changes in how the headphones are worn.

Figure 5: Noise reduction of the fixed, adaptive and semi-adaptive ANC systems with a time-varying secondary path

Figure 5 shows the noise reduction of the fixed (black line), adaptive (blue line) and semi-adaptive (red line) ANC systems as the secondary path varies over time. Note that the noise reduction shown here is not broken down by frequency. As we said before, ANC performance depends strongly on frequency: noise reduction is generally much greater at low frequencies than at high ones. The y-axis shows the attenuated noise level; the x-axis is simulation time, 10 seconds in all, with the secondary path G(z) switched every two seconds. G2(z) and G4(z) are secondary paths measured in two special cases: the headphones not fully covering the ears, and lying on a table.

As you can see, the fixed ANC system’s noise reduction is unremarkable but very robust. When the secondary path switches, there is no big jump in residual noise. In the two special cases, its noise reduction becomes very weak, because the actual G(z) now differs considerably from the Ĝ(z) used when the filter was designed. Now the adaptive ANC system. While G(z) stays the same, its noise reduction improves over time until it reaches a steady state. But when G(z) switches, a large residual noise suddenly appears (active noise cancellation abruptly turns into active noise amplification), and it takes a while to adapt back. Imagine a sudden screech right in your ear. What would you do? Throw the headphones, that’s what! Nobody knows how users will treat their headphones, so a fully adaptive design is risky. That is why almost all ANC headphones on the market are fixed designs, and any adaptive ones come with plenty of constraints and rules on the adaptation. (If anyone knows a consumer headphone on the market that is adaptive, please let me know~)

Now the semi-adaptive ANC system. It clearly strikes a compromise. Its noise reduction still can’t match the adaptive system’s, but it is very stable and doesn’t produce a sudden burst of residual noise when the secondary path switches. It takes the strength of the fixed system, its stability, while reducing noise better than the fixed filter does.

The point of this article is not to show off the new ANC system I proposed, but to use a concrete simulation to show the strengths and weaknesses of adaptive and fixed ANC systems, and one possible way to improve on them. There is still plenty of room to improve the semi-adaptive filter, for example by changing how the weight a is calculated or by combining the filters in other ways.

For the details, please see the published paper. Suggestions and comments are always welcome.

Author: S.Li

PhD in acoustics from Germany, now working in China~ Main research topics include stereo, binaural audio, psychoacoustics and active noise cancellation. Always happy to hang out and talk shop with anyone working on similar topics ^_^
